opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The Alberta Plan, for me, is really a research roadmap more than a recipe. It's something Rich Sutton, Mike Bowling, and I put together to lay out how we think we can make steady, cumulative progress toward understanding intelligence, and specifically toward building agents that understand and interact with the world in a rich, flexible way.

At its core is a commitment to a particular perspective: intelligence is about an agent interacting with a vastly complex world, getting a stream of experience, taking actions, and trying to achieve goals, which in the reinforcement learning view are captured by reward. Everything the agent knows, it should ideally learn from that ongoing experience. So the plan emphasizes continual learning. The agent isn't trained once and frozen. It's learning all the time, in real time, from its own interaction.

A big part of it is the idea that the world is far larger than the agent. You can never model everything perfectly, so the agent has to build approximate, useful knowledge: predictions about what will happen, models of how the world responds to its actions, and the ability to plan with those models. The plan lays out a sequence of steps, starting with representation learning and continual prediction, then control, then building up to model-based planning and what we call the "STOMP" progression of subtasks, options, models, and planning. The goal is an architecture where the agent creates its own features, its own subproblems, and its own abstractions.

From my side, coming from a background in rehabilitation robotics and prosthetics, this resonates deeply. When you put a learning system on a prosthetic arm attached to a person, you can't pre-train it for every situation. That person's life changes day to day, their body changes, their goals change. The system has to adapt continually, build predictions about what the person is going to do next, and work with them as a partner. That's a microcosm of what the Alberta Plan is about: agents that learn from experience, in the moment, alongside the people and environments they're embedded in.

So I'd describe it as a bet on a principled, experience-driven path to AGI, focused on the fundamentals of how a mind can grow its understanding over time, rather than scaling up a static system trained on fixed datasets. It's not the only path, but it's one we think gets at the heart of what intelligence actually is.

r001.rationale: It makes learning from the agent’s ongoing experience and interaction with the world central to the plan.

r002.rationale: It describes the plan as a research roadmap and explains its agent architecture, but does not clearly distinguish that framework from commitments about how research should be conducted.

r003.rationale: It names the plan’s three authors but does not characterize it as an agenda involving researchers they have never met.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about the Alberta Plan is that it's really a research roadmap, a twelve-step program, in a sense, for building intelligent agents that learn continually from their own experience. It came out of a collaboration between Rich Sutton, Mike Bowling, and myself, and the core of it is a very particular stance on what intelligence is and how it should be built.

The starting point is the idea of an agent that interacts with a world through a stream of experience. It gets observations, it takes actions, it receives rewards, and it has to make sense of all of that online, in real time, with a fixed amount of computation at each step. That's the setting we care about. Not a batch of data that gets processed offline, and not a model that gets trained once and then frozen, but a system that is always learning, always updating, and that has to be able to keep learning for as long as it's running. Continual learning is right at the heart of it.

From there the plan lays out a sequence of components that we think an intelligent agent needs. You start with representation, how the agent builds up features of the world from raw sensorimotor experience. Then there's prediction, and this is where ideas like general value functions come in, the notion that an agent can have many, many predictions about what will happen to its own experience stream, and that these predictions become a kind of knowledge. Then there's control, learning what to do to achieve goals. And then you move into model-based reasoning, planning, options or temporally extended actions, and ultimately an agent that can build a model of its world, plan with it, and keep refining it from experience.

One thing I'd emphasize is that the plan is deliberately modest in its claims about what is already solved. Each step identifies problems that we think are genuinely open, like how to do representation learning in a truly continual way without forgetting, or how to make planning tractable with learned models that are imperfect. And it's meant to be followed roughly in order, because each step builds on the capabilities of the one before it.

The other thing I'd say is that it's a bet on simplicity and on first principles. Rather than bolting together a lot of special-purpose modules, the idea is that a small number of general learning mechanisms, applied consistently, can scale up to very rich behaviour. That's a different path than some of the current large-scale approaches, and we see it as complementary rather than in competition. But for us, if you want something that deserves the name artificial general intelligence, it has to be an agent that can learn anything from its own experience over a lifetime, and the Alberta Plan is our attempt to say concretely what the path to that looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligent agents should continually learn online from their own sensorimotor experience and interactions with the world.

r002.rationale: It describes both the agent-building framework (representation, prediction, control, and planning) and research commitments such as addressing open problems, following the steps roughly in order, and favoring general mechanisms.

r003.rationale: It identifies the three collaborators but does not characterize the plan as a shared agenda that can include researchers its authors have never met.

astra-6.text:
I understand the Alberta Plan as a research agenda organized around a fairly simple idea: intelligence grows out of interaction. An agent acts in the world, observes the consequences, and learns how to do better over time. Reinforcement learning gives us a framework for studying that process.

The challenge is to connect that learning process to the other capabilities we associate with intelligence. How does an agent build a useful representation of its experience? How does it learn a model of the world, use that model to plan, and develop abstractions that help it solve new problems? Those capabilities need to work together in an agent that keeps learning, rather than being designed separately and then frozen.

What I find compelling is that this makes the pursuit of general intelligence a concrete scientific program. You can start with relatively simple agents, investigate the pieces, and progressively bring them together. The ambition is broad, but the approach is incremental: understand how experience can produce increasingly capable behavior.

r001.rationale: It says intelligence grows from an agent acting, observing consequences, and learning to improve over time.

r002.rationale: It presents reinforcement learning as a framework for studying agent learning, then separately describes the research approach as incremental: studying simpler agents and progressively combining capabilities.

r003.rationale: It calls the Alberta Plan a research agenda but does not say it is shared among participants, including researchers its authors have never met.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the Alberta Plan as a roadmap for understanding how an agent can learn to become intelligent through interaction with its world. The starting point is a continual stream of experience: an agent takes actions, receives observations and rewards, and has to learn while that interaction is happening.

A central idea is that intelligence should be built around that ongoing process, rather than treating learning as something that happens once, on a fixed dataset, before the system is deployed. The agent needs to learn what to predict, how to represent its experience, and how to act. Those capabilities have to work together under real limits on computation and memory.

The plan lays out a progression from simpler learning problems toward increasingly capable agents. So I see it as a research program: build the foundations, understand them, and then bring prediction, control, representation, and planning together. The ambition is that the same principles can support an agent that keeps learning and becomes competent across a broad range of situations.

r001.rationale: It says the agent learns through its own ongoing interaction with the world, taking actions and receiving observations and rewards.

r002.rationale: It describes both the agent-learning framework and the research program for building foundations and integrating capabilities.

r003.rationale: It calls the plan a research program but does not say it is a shared agenda that can include researchers its authors have never met.
